notes: Original lectures (batch 1 of 3). Each lecture feeds eight types: RL, SST, LMCMA, LFIB, HCS, LMCSA, SMW and HIW. Lectures 11 to 15 are backup questions.

sources.title: Sleep and memory
sources.body: Why do students who sleep well after studying remember more? Research suggests that the brain does not simply rest at night. During deep sleep, the hippocampus replays patterns of activity from the day, and this replay appears to transfer new information into longer-term storage in the cortex. In a well-known type of experiment, participants learn a list of word pairs in the evening. Those who sleep normally recall more pairs the next morning than those kept awake, even when both groups are tested at the same time of day. Dreaming sleep may play a different role, helping people connect ideas and regulate emotion. The practical message for learners is simple: staying up all night before an exam may weaken the very memories they are trying to build.

sources.title: Kauri dieback in New Zealand
sources.body: Kauri are among the largest and longest-living trees in the world, and they grow naturally only in the northern part of New Zealand. Since the early two thousands, many kauri have been killed by a disease known as kauri dieback. It is caused by a microscopic organism that lives in the soil and attacks the roots, slowly starving the tree of water and nutrients. There is no cure, and infected trees almost always die. Because the organism spreads in soil, even a small amount of mud on a shoe can carry it from one forest to another. For this reason, many tracks have been closed or rebuilt with raised boardwalks, and visitors are asked to clean their footwear at stations on the way in and out. Protecting kauri, the speaker argues, depends largely on changing everyday behaviour.

sources.title: The printing press and the spread of ideas
sources.body: Before the fifteenth century, most books in Europe were copied by hand, which made them slow to produce and very expensive. The printing press with movable metal type changed this dramatically. A single workshop could now produce hundreds of identical copies of a text in the time it once took to copy a few. Historians point to several consequences. First, prices fell, so books reached merchants and professionals, not only the church and the nobility. Second, identical copies meant that scholars in different cities could refer to exactly the same page, which made debate and correction easier. Third, printing helped standardise spelling and grammar in many languages. However, printing did not create literacy on its own; schools and cheaper paper were also essential. Technology, in other words, rarely transforms society without support from other changes.

sources.title: Ocean acidification and shellfish
sources.body: The oceans absorb roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide that humans release into the atmosphere. This slows climate change, but it comes at a cost. When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, and the water gradually becomes more acidic. This process reduces the amount of carbonate available to animals that build shells or skeletons, such as oysters, mussels and many types of plankton. Young shellfish are especially vulnerable because they must build their shells quickly in the first days of life. Some oyster hatcheries have already reported mass deaths of larvae when acidic water was pumped into their tanks. Hatcheries now monitor water chemistry closely and adjust it before use. In the long term, however, the speaker stresses that the only lasting solution is to reduce carbon emissions at their source.

sources.title: Default options and saving for retirement
sources.body: Traditional economics assumes that people carefully compare options and choose what is best for them. Behavioural economists have shown that real decisions are often shaped by something much simpler: the default, or what happens if we do nothing. Retirement saving is a clear example. When employees must actively sign up for a workplace savings scheme, many never get around to it, even if they intend to. When they are enrolled automatically and must actively opt out, participation rises sharply. New Zealand used this idea when it introduced KiwiSaver, which automatically enrols new employees while allowing them to leave. Critics argue that defaults can be used to push people towards choices that benefit organisations rather than individuals. Supporters reply that some default is unavoidable, so it should at least be designed with people's long-term interests in mind.

sources.title: Does bilingualism change the brain?
sources.body: For many years, researchers claimed that speaking two languages gives people a general cognitive advantage. The argument was that bilingual speakers constantly suppress one language while using the other, and that this practice strengthens the brain's control systems. Early studies found that bilingual children performed better on tasks that required switching attention or ignoring distractions. More recent research has been more cautious. Several large studies have failed to find consistent differences, and some researchers suggest that earlier results were influenced by small samples and by differences in income or education between groups. This does not mean bilingualism has no benefits. It clearly offers social, cultural and economic advantages, and it may help delay the symptoms of dementia. The speaker concludes that the benefits of bilingualism are real, but they may be more social than cognitive.

sources.title: Urban heat islands
sources.body: Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a pattern known as the urban heat island effect. There are three main causes. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofing absorb sunlight during the day and release heat at night. Buildings trap warm air and reduce wind. And human activity, from car engines to air conditioners, adds extra heat directly. The effect matters because heatwaves are becoming more frequent, and high night-time temperatures are particularly dangerous for older people. Cities are responding in different ways. Some paint roofs white to reflect sunlight, while others plant street trees or create small parks that provide shade and cool the air through evaporation. Western Sydney, one of the hottest parts of that city, has set targets to increase tree cover. These measures work best when they are planned together.

sources.title: Coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef
sources.body: Corals get their colour, and most of their energy, from tiny algae that live inside their tissues. When water becomes too warm for too long, this partnership breaks down. The coral expels the algae and turns white, a process called bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving, and if the water does not cool within a few weeks, it may die. The Great Barrier Reef has experienced several mass bleaching events since the late nineteen nineties, and the gaps between them have become shorter. This matters because corals need years to recover, and fast-growing species tend to return first, which changes the structure of the reef. Scientists are testing ways to help, such as breeding heat-tolerant corals. Nevertheless, most reef scientists agree that without lower emissions, these efforts can only buy time.

sources.title: Antibiotic resistance
sources.body: Antibiotics have saved millions of lives, but their effectiveness is declining. Bacteria reproduce very quickly, and random genetic changes sometimes allow a few of them to survive a particular drug. When antibiotics are used, the sensitive bacteria die and the resistant ones multiply. Over time, the resistant strain can become dominant. Some bacteria can even pass resistance genes to other species. Two practices speed this up. The first is prescribing antibiotics for illnesses they cannot treat, such as common colds caused by viruses. The second is the routine use of antibiotics in farm animals to promote growth. At the same time, very few new antibiotics are being developed, partly because they are less profitable than medicines taken for many years. The speaker argues that governments must reward companies for developing new antibiotics that are then used as rarely as possible.

sources.title: The promise and limits of microfinance
sources.body: Microfinance means providing very small loans to people who cannot borrow from ordinary banks, usually because they have no property to offer as security. In the nineteen seventies and eighties, pioneers of the idea lent small sums to groups of women in rural Bangladesh, who used the money to start or expand small businesses. Repayment rates were surprisingly high, partly because group members supported and encouraged one another. The model spread rapidly around the world and was widely praised as a tool for ending poverty. Later, carefully designed studies painted a more modest picture. Access to loans helped some households manage risk and invest, but average incomes did not rise dramatically. In some regions, borrowers took several loans at once and fell into debt. Microfinance, the speaker concludes, is a useful financial service rather than a cure for poverty.

sources.title: Retreating glaciers in the Southern Alps
sources.body: New Zealand's Southern Alps contain thousands of glaciers, and scientists have photographed many of them from the air at the end of every summer since the late nineteen seventies. These surveys show that the total volume of ice has fallen substantially. The loss is not steady. Some years, heavy winter snowfall allowed a few glaciers to advance, but warm summers have increasingly outweighed these gains. The retreat has several effects. Glacier tourism has had to adapt, because some famous glaciers can no longer be reached safely on foot, so visitors now often arrive by helicopter. Meltwater from glaciers also feeds rivers used for hydroelectric power and irrigation, so long-term changes could affect water supply. The speaker notes that glaciers respond to climate more clearly than almost any other natural system, which makes them valuable early warning signals.

sources.title: The placebo effect
sources.body: A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill. Surprisingly, patients who receive placebos often report real improvements, particularly for symptoms like pain, nausea and fatigue. This is called the placebo effect. Part of it is explained by expectation. When people believe a treatment will help, the brain can release natural painkillers and change how signals from the body are interpreted. The setting also matters. A caring doctor, a longer consultation and even the colour or price of a pill can increase the effect. Because of this, new medicines are tested against placebos rather than against no treatment at all. A drug is only considered effective if it performs better than the placebo. Interestingly, some studies suggest placebos can work even when patients are told honestly what they are taking.

sources.title: Resilient supply chains
sources.body: For decades, many companies organised their supply chains around efficiency. They kept very little stock, relied on a small number of low-cost suppliers, and scheduled deliveries to arrive just before they were needed. This approach reduced costs, but it also made businesses fragile. When a factory closed, a port was congested or a ship blocked a major canal, shortages spread quickly around the world. Since then, many firms have started to value resilience alongside efficiency. Some now buy parts from suppliers in more than one country, while others hold larger safety stocks of critical components. Digital tools that map every supplier, not just the direct ones, are also becoming common. These changes increase costs, so companies must decide how much disruption they can tolerate. The speaker suggests that the right balance depends on the product.

sources.title: Why pollinators matter
sources.body: About three quarters of the world's major food crops benefit to some extent from animal pollination. Bees are the best known pollinators, but flies, beetles, moths, birds and bats also play important roles. When a pollinator visits a flower to feed on nectar, pollen sticks to its body and is carried to the next flower, allowing the plant to produce seeds and fruit. In many regions, pollinator populations have declined. The main causes include the loss of wild flowering habitat, certain pesticides, parasites and diseases, and changes in climate that disrupt the timing between flowering and insect activity. Farmers can respond by planting strips of wildflowers beside crops and by reducing pesticide use during flowering. The speaker emphasises that relying on managed honeybees alone is risky, because wild pollinators are often more effective for many crops.

sources.title: Language nests and language revival
sources.body: When a language has few young speakers, it is at risk of disappearing within a few generations. One of the most influential responses to this problem began in New Zealand in the early nineteen eighties with kōhanga reo, or language nests. In these early childhood centres, young children are cared for entirely in te reo Māori, often by older fluent speakers. The idea was simple but powerful: children acquire languages most easily when they are immersed in them from an early age. The model later expanded into primary and secondary schools that teach in Māori. It has also inspired similar programmes for Hawaiian and other indigenous languages. Researchers point out that schools alone cannot save a language. Revival is most successful when the language is also used at home and in the wider community.
